newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW - State debt tough for Finland's Niinisto.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - State debt tough for Finland's Niinisto.

text.p: Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said on Thursday Finland meets all convergence criteria and would join Europe's single currency union, but emphasised that he could not rest easy as state debt was still an acute problem.

Gross public debt and the general government deficit relative to GDP had been "with a high degree of probability" inside the EMU-limits already last year and would "certainly" be safely inside in 1997, Niinisto told Reuters in an interview.
"But we have no reason to exult, to believe that we are home free. Our state debt is a burning problem," Niinisto said.
The finance ministry forecasts a steep rise in state debt since 1991 will level out this year at around 72 percent of gross domestic product.

At the end of 1990, before the onset of the severest recession since World War Two, Finnish state debt at 54 billion markka was 10.5 percent of GDP. At the end of 1997, state debt is projected at 430 billion markka or nearly 72 percent of GDP, according to the national budget.
State 1997 net borrowing is forecast at some 28 billion markka. Last year, state net borrowing was 34 billion markka, some five billion markka less than forecast early in 1996.

"The trend has been favourable. But we have not seen any radical turnaround," Niinisto said. Spending in 1998-99, the coalition government's remaining two years in office, would not be allowed to rise beyond earlier agreed tight frames.
Niinisto said Finland would be forced to remain a net borrower well into next millennium.
"Measured by state debt we are among the three worst EU countries," Niinisto said. "For us, the EMU (deficit and debt) criteria are very easy, far too easy," he said.
Gross public debt should be at most 60 percent of GDP and the public deficit at most three percent of GDP.
In November, the Finnish finance ministry said stronger than expected growth and a more favourable debt structure would bring gross public debt below 60 percent of GDP already in 1996.
Its current official forecast, from September, put the 1997 EMU debt at 61.0 percent of GDP, down from 61.8 percent in 1996.
Finland's EMU debt is smaller than the state debt because work pension funds' holdings of state paper are deducted from the state's total outstanding debt.
The deficit -- projected by the ministry at 1.4 percent of GDP in 1997 and 2.9 percent in 1996 -- is clearly smaller than the state finance deficit at 5.1 and 6.9 percent respectively.

Asked whether he was confident Finland would be among the countries joining the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union in the first wave, Niinisto said it was unlikely that any other EU member state would reject Finnish membership.
"Our approach has been that we aim to put our affairs in order so that we meet all criteria. That hurdle we have now left behind," he said.
EU leaders are due to decide in spring 1998 which countries will join the single currency, scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999.
"I have no reason to doubt the timetable," Niinisto said.
Niinisto said he expected the national parliament to vote in favour of Finnish membership of EMU.
One or more indicative votes on EMU-related issues were likely already this spring ahead of the formal parliamentary decision scheduled late this year or early 1998, he said.
"I think that the going-in side will win," he said.
